title: Role of matriptase in corneal epithelial homeostasis and repair
text:
Injuries or diseases involving the cornea, the protective outer layer of the eye, can lead to infection,
inflammation, and vision impairment which greatly affect the quality of life for patients. The key objective of
the current project is to identify the molecular and cellular mechanisms that ensure maintenance of a healthy
and functional cornea, as well as the natural processes that facilitate corneal self-repair. This knowledge will
be used to develop new treatments for patients with corneal injury and/or disease.

title: Childhood Infections Research Program
text:
The Childhood Infections Research Program (CHIRP) for 14 years has trained and facilitated the career
development of investigators studying infectious diseases relevant to children. The outcomes will be
investigators who will make a long-term impact on the fundamental biology, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment
of infections or infection-related complications in children. We anticipate high public health relevance due to a
sustained and direct impact on the health of children.

title: Vanderbilt Center of Excellence for Undiagnosed Disease (VCEUD)
text: Our proposed VCEUD (Vanderbilt Center of Excellence in Undiagnosed Diseases) will function in the broader Undiagnosed Disease Network to identify the cause of undiagnosed diseases and thus help patients and their families. We will work with local communities and organizations to increase the recruitment of underserved and minority patients into UDN. We will also work with UDN to develop more powerful AI-based tools and resources to make diagnosing undiagnosed diseases more efficient and to help doctors find people with undiagnosed conditions more easily.

title: Using Computer Vision to Improve the Evaluation of Dysplasia in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
text:
Dysplasia detection in inflammatory bowel disease is difficult to detect on colonoscopy and histology due to non-
uniform appearance, confounding concurrent inflammation, and lesion sparsity. Computer vision methods can
be used to not only model the visual characteristics predictive of histologically-proven dysplasia, but also can be
trained to quantify features that define the presence and grade of dysplasia. Computer vision systems for both
colonoscopy and histology are likely to exceed expert performance for detecting dysplasia that will help to: (1)
standardize surveillance strategies, (2) better define dysplasia severity grading, and (3) elevate the performance
of less experienced endoscopists in screening for dysplasia in IBD.

title: Uncovering Novel Regulatory Pathways and Functions of the Telomerase RNA Component in the Hematopoietic System
text:
Mutations that impact the stability of telomerase RNA molecules are found in most cases of patients suffering
from the bone marrow failure syndrome dyskeratosis congenita. In this proposal our goal is to identify novel
molecular mechanisms that can be controlled to prevent that mutations found in these patients cause reduced
RNA stability, which will rescue hematopoietic development and improve quality of life. We will use a unique
combination of molecular and cellular tools that will significantly increase current knowledge on telomerase RNA
stability and function in hematopoietic cells that are deficient in patients with bone marrow failure.

title: Mechanical Regulation of Cell Fate and Multi-Scale Function in the Developing Meniscus
text:
The meniscus plays a vital role in knee function and is prone to injury, but the cellular mechanisms regulating its
development, maturation and maintenance are poorly understood. This project seeks to fill this knowledge gap
by elucidating the role of cellular force generation and mechanosensing in regulating embryonic meniscus
patterning, cell fate determination and matrix specialization during embryonic-to-early postnatal growth, and in
maintaining cell phenotype in the adult meniscus. Results will establish the mechanobiological basis that
regulates the meniscus development and homeostasis, providing new insight to direct regenerative strategies.

title: Chloride channels in endothelial cells
text:
Endothelial cells regulate arterial contractility. Dysfunctional control of contractility by endothelial
cells is a hallmark of several cardiovascular diseases, including hypertension, but pathological
mechanisms involved are poorly understood. We will investigate the novel hypothesis that
TMEM16A channels regulate arterial contractility, investigate signaling mechanisms involved
and test the concept that vasodilation mediated by these proteins is dysfunctional during
hypertension.

title: Pathobiology of Cholestatic Liver Disease
text:
This proposal examines the mechanisms by which infiltrating immune cells (neutrophils) promote inflammation
and scarring in Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC), a liver disease with no effective medical therapy. We will
investigate and target the mechanisms of neutrophil recruitment, retention, and activation that lead to
inflammation and scarring in preclinical studies. Thus, the work has the potential to identify new therapeutic
strategies to treat patients with this debilitating liver disease.

title: Lysine Methylation as a Novel Regulatory Mechanism of HPV E2 Function
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on understanding E2 lysine methylation
throughout the replicative human papillomavirus (HPV) lifecycle. New insights in host-viral interactions will
provide direct targets and treatments against persistent HPV infections. This application is relevant to NIAID’s
mission to understand and prevent infectious diseases.

title: Defining the Interplay Between Viral Adaptation and Host Proteostasis
text: Understanding the factors that shape the extraordinary capacity of RNA viruses like influenza to adapt to selection pressures, ranging from the immune system, to drugs, to new host environments upon zoonotic transmission, is critical for predicting and preventing pathologic viral adaptation and designing effective antiviral drugs and vaccines. By assisting the folding of otherwise defective viral protein variants, hijacked host cell protein folding machineries play a critical role in defining what evolutionary trajectories are available to a virus as it adapts to selection pressures. The proposed research aims to illuminate this phenomenon at the molecular and genomic levels, greatly improving understanding of viral adaptation and evolution at the host- pathogen interface in a way that will not only be fundamentally important but also likely prove valuable in the long-term for the design of novel antiviral strategies.

title: Development of an Automated Sample Preparation Platform for High Throughput Mass Spectrometry Characterization of Biotherapeutics
text:
As biotherapeutics become increasingly complex to address challenging diseases, the need for more
sophisticated characterization drives up manufacturing and development costs, ultimately leading to expensive
treatments and limited patient access. To address these critical barriers, the Auto-DynaChip platform transforms
mass spectrometry characterization – the gold standard for biotherapeutic analysis – by seamlessly integrating
microfluidic sample preparation with nanoflow electrospray ionization, unlocking advanced techniques like native
mass spectrometry and charge detection mass spectrometry that reveal critical molecular details previously
inaccessible in routine biotherapeutic characterization workflows. By making these sophisticated
characterization methods accessible and high-throughput, the Auto-DynaChip delivers deeper molecular
understanding on more samples than before, ultimately accelerating therapeutic development, improving drug
quality, and increasing patient accessibility to life-saving medicines.

title: CTSA Predoctoral T32 at Boston University
text:
There is a growing and pressing national need for regenerative and stem cell-based therapies that can replenish
organs, tissues, or cells damaged by disease, injuries, infections, or gene mutations. To meet these needs,
commonly referred to as “regenerative medicine”, here we propose a predoctoral “Regenerative Medicine
Training Program” (RMTP) designed to provide rigorous training in all aspects of translational research related
to this rapidly emerging field. The goal of the RMTP is to prepare the next generation of creative and responsible
transdisciplinary translational scientists who will serve as thought leaders to spearhead national efforts to bring
regenerative medicine into widespread clinical practice.

title: Southern African-Pittsburgh Public Health Genomic Epidemiology Training Program (SAPPHGenE)
text: We propose to continue the highly-successful Southern Africa-Pittsburgh Public Health Genomic Epidemiology Research Training Program (SAPPHGenE) in the areas of bacterial pneumonia, invasive bacterial diseases, respiratory viruses, and fungal infections. This will be accomplished by an expert, multidisciplinary team of research mentors at the University of Pittsburgh and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta. The ultimate goal of the program is to prevent and control these diseases, some of which are vaccine preventable and all which are major causes of morbidity and mortality in the United States, Southern Africa, and globally.

title: Decoding epigenetic adapters of cell state
text:
Pluripotent stem cells have the amazing potential to differentiate into any somatic cell type enabled by an open
chromatin structure. The absence of cell identity-enforcing heterochromatin amplifies transcriptional output, a
phenomenon broadly observed in lineage stem cells and cancer stem cells. We will develop a research
program that mechanistically interrogates the interconnected network of epigenetic modifications, global
transcription, and developmental potential across cell states.

title: Resources,  Workforce Development, and Animal Models for the Rutgers RBL
text:
Overall - PROJECT NARRATIVE
This proposal will enhance the capabilities of the Rutgers Regional Biocontainment Laboratory to respond to the
next public health emergency or pandemic by supporting efficient operations and maintenance of its high-level
biosafety laboratory facilities, training and maintaining critical faculty and staff, developing and disseminating
state-of-the art safety and disaster response procedures, and developing scientific models of disease.

title: Evolutionary Conserved Mechanisms that Control Central Nervous System Development Regeneration and Degeneration
text:
In this proposal we will investigate the stepwise cellular and genetic changes that control central nervous system
development, regeneration and aging using a unique long-lived invertebrate model organism, Botryllus
schlosseri, that reproduces both sexually as chordates and asexually as invertebrates and undergoes weekly
degeneration and regeneration of its CNS during its adult life.
Focusing on Botryllus brain cells we will characterize the genes and programs involved in the development of
sexually produced larval brains, and asexually produced adult brains, isolate neural stem cells, and determine
the difference between brain development and regeneration.
Additional comparisons between the neural stem cells of young (< 6 months) and old (> 7 years) Botryllus
colonies, will shed light on the process of neurodegeneration and neural stem cell aging.

title: Site 3/3, Understanding PTSD through Postmortem Targeted Brain Multiomics
text:
The prevalence of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression are among the most common of the
severe major psychiatric disorders. There have yet to be postmortem studies of well-matched cases and controls
to leverage the fact that these are arguably among the best understood psychiatric disorders in terms of neural
circuit regulation. Building on impactful linked R01 project, in our renewal proposal we will expand the sample
size and dive deeper with more detailed analyses of the postmortem phenotypes and more comprehensive mo-
lecular studies to identify pathways harboring potential diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: An Ancestry-Informed Approach to Improve Genetic Testing for Cardiovascular Disease
text: Genetic testing for cardiovascular disease (CVD) and elevated lipoprotein a is now being implemented in-clinic to prevent disease and save lives, yet we are still far away from genetic testing being a first-line tool given existing gaps in accuracy. This is the case as many genetic tests do not stratify patient risk well across the full US populace. My project aims to fill this gap and attain improved and personalized prediction of CVD, doing so through fine-scale studies of linkage disequilibrium, gene discovery approaches, and the construction of a novel risk prediction method integrating variants of large effect alongside polygenic variation.

title: Project 1: Employing CD11b-Agonists to Render PDAC Responsive to Immunotherapy
text: These studies seek to understand if targeting integrins on myeloid cells can impact therapeutic responsiveness to immunotherapy in pancreas cancer. They include studies clinically testing an integrin agonist in PDAC patients and correlative and laboratory studies to understand mechanism of resistance.

title: Cellular and biophysical interactions to build oocyte-follicle complexes
text:
Oocytes, which are the precursors to egg cells, develop in the ovary in structures called follicles where they are
wrapped in somatic granulosa cells. In this project, I will study how granulosa cells move to form follicles
around newly-developing oocytes, how this process is affected by the physical environment of the ovary, and
how oocytes and granulosa cells communicate with each other. This will inform future studies of reproductive
aging, conditions such as polycystic ovarian syndrome, and the development of assisted reproductive
therapies such as IVF.
